source_location: Thesis title p.1; site description l.~700; charcoal fire history chapter

evidence: Paper models topographic controls on persistent fire refugia in the Canadian Rocky Mountains (Banff area); no post-fire debris flows, thresholds, volume models or warning systems; Colorado appears only in reference titles.
note: Relevant to Rocky Mountains generally but provides none of the attributed debris-flow science; Canadian not Colorado.

source_location: Abstract; Sect. 'Seasonality and origin' l.1265-1280; study area l.119-120

note: Winter fires supported; foehn valleys not stated (only drying fall winds in south). Foehn-region winter fires appear in Muller 2020 citing Schunk 2013.

evidence: Mediterranean review: wildfires lower destination attractiveness and visitor numbers; nothing on Alpine visitor calendars, shortened snow cover or summer influx of heat-escaping visitors.

evidence: Global review used a Scopus/Web of Science keyword search restricted to English-language papers; authors note the search may have missed some literature. No citation chaining, starting documents, or discussion of multilingual national technical reports.

evidence: Catalan wildfire-prevention subsidies funded by CO2 tax on vehicles, budgets EUR 5000-200,000 per proposal; managed area after three calls covers 3.87% of 151,195.99 ha strategic area.
note: Numbers match (151,196 rounded).

evidence: Interaction of upper winds with rugged terrain produces highly variable, turbulent winds; the assumed fire-weather continuum has reduced validity; danger ratings traditionally use synoptic-scale observations.
note: Sharples' share (terrain controls surface wind) clearly supported; the 'danger systems omit terrain' half rests mainly on the co-cited key.

evidence: Rockfall risk reduction by a Valais protection forest expressed in CHF per year (~1,350 CHF per ha forest per year), tracked under climate scenarios with species shifts.
note: Monetised valuation of protective service confirmed.

evidence: Spalling 'occurred equally in areas of high and moderate high burn severity; was sparse in areas of moderate low and low severity' (Montiferru 2021, Sardinia).
note: Matches; 'did not differ' paraphrases 'occurred equally' (no formal test implied).

evidence: Autumn 2011 Bavarian Alps: persistent inversion with thermal belt gave warmer, drier mid-slope conditions, massive fuel drying and mid-slope fires, contrasted by moderate danger in valleys; not resolved by standard stations.
note: Matches closely.

evidence: Upper winds interacting with rugged terrain yield variable, turbulent wind and discontinuous emergent properties; the 'fire weather continuum' is of reduced validity; station placement matters.
note: Valley-floor interpolation is a fair application of the stated reduced validity.

evidence: Austrian IFDS validated with 2018-2019 fires: some variants gave better ignition prediction accuracy than common fire weather indices, but correlation between larger burned areas and higher index values was low.
note: Matches.

evidence: RdNBR calibrated with CBI used to map severity; no proportionality between fire-induced soil changes and severity class; strongest water repellency mostly in low-severity plots; severity maps can fail to identify most severely burnt soils.
note: Negri's share (severity decoupled from soil hydrological condition) supported; phenology/illumination bias belongs to co-cited keys.

evidence: 'Command and control' approach in fire management neglects the fundamental role fire regimes have in sustaining biodiversity and key ecosystem services; context-specific, place-based approaches and land-use planning needed.
note: Near-verbatim support.

evidence: Austrian building wildfire vulnerability index weighted by AHP with national and international experts; indicators in three categories: building environment (6), building exterior (7), building characteristics (8) = 21.
note: Counts and grouping match.

evidence: IFDS for Austria combines daily fire weather index, human-ignition hazard map, lightning fire hazard map, high-resolution fuel type map and topography-based hazard; improves ignition prediction but low correlation with burned area.
note: Matches the table row.

evidence: Hazard projected to rise most in northern/eastern Alps; 'there will be a stronger need for the development of pre-fire management strategies in the currently less affected areas of the European Alps'.
note: Anticipation framing is a fair paraphrase.
